title: What MemSpine should build: multiple layers on a small token budget
intro: Drawn from the 15 code-traced records. The field converges on one shape: keep raw turns as cheap, durable truth; derive compact layers in the background; read with no LLM call under a hard token budget; keep agentic reading as an opt-in tier. Everything below fits the write design already decided (adaptive window, three call slots, at most one call per turn, facts then summary then graph then episodes).

sections.title: 1. What most strong engines agree on
items: Raw turns stored at once with no LLM call, derived layers built later: MemMachine, Mnemon, MemOS (fast-then-fine), Memori, Honcho, MemSpine.

No LLM call on the hot read path: Hindsight, Honcho get_context, MemMachine, Memori, Nemori, memU, Mem0, MemSpine. Agentic reading is a separate, opt-in tier (Honcho dialectic levels, MemMachine agent mode, EverMemOS decider).

Write-time LLM work is batched by token window or episode, never per turn: LightMem (512-token buffer), Honcho (1,024-token window), MemOS (1,024-token window), Nemori (episode), MemSpine (adaptive window).
Updates and contradictions move to background consolidation: Hindsight observations, Honcho dreamer, LightMem similarity-gated update, Mnemon fold, Cognee contradicts / superseded edges.

Small contexts come from a hard budget, not from luck: Mnemon 16 items / 12,000 chars (3.8k tokens, 91.7 self-reported), Hindsight token-denominated packing, MemOS relevance floor + MMR + per-type quotas, Nemori two compact layers (2.7k). The one engine without a budget (Cognee) sends 32.5k tokens per question.
Our own f-slot screen agrees: an always-available agentic loop cost about 8x the time for net -3 on the focus slice, so agentic reading stays opt-in.

sections.title: 4. Engineering for speed and safety on the write path
items: Durable window queue: stage a cursor at prepare, promote it only on commit, so a crash re-offers windows instead of losing them (memU). Fixes our open caveat that the window queue is not durable.
Plan-embed-write commit: batch every embedding of a derived write into one call before anything is written, so a failed commit is a no-op (memU).
Diff-based re-embedding: hash content and re-embed only what changed (memU, EverMemOS).

Optional local pre-compression of the window transcript with a token classifier (LLMLingua-2) before call 1, cutting extractor prompt tokens 20-40% (LightMem). Screen it: it can drop a detail the fact needed.
Similarity-gated consolidation: only fact pairs above about 0.9 cosine go to the LLM; everything else is free (LightMem).
Background triggers by volume and idleness, not per write: for example 50 new facts, 60 minutes idle, at most every 8 hours (Honcho).
Per-stage call, token and latency counters reported next to accuracy (LightMem, Nemori, MemMachine); MemSpine has window_stats and model_usage, extend them to every layer.

sections.title: 5. Read path additions to screen
items: Contextualised rerank: score the whole neighbour window, not the single turn, then fill best-first (MemMachine).
Rule-based temporal window from the question (dateparser-style) as its own leg (Hindsight, MIRIX); MemSpine's temporal leg covers absolute dates only.
Rule-based query router that sends date-scoped questions to a temporal path at no LLM cost (Cognee); MemSpine's question shape can drive it.
Cheap batched yes/no screening of a wide pool before the reader (Mnemon's Jev; MemSpine's local OpenDecider is the in-house analogue).
Write absolute dates into derived text at write time ('yesterday (2023-05-07)') while raw turns stay untouched (Nemori, EverMemOS, Cognee timestamp nodes).

sections.title: 6. Do not copy
items: Overwriting or deleting a value with no history (MIRIX, Honcho, LightMem, MemOS forgetting by count). MemSpine keeps supersede / contest with as-of reads.
Ingestion time used as event time (Memori, Nemori). MemSpine stamps valid_from from the turn.
No context budget (Cognee, 32.5k tokens per question).
Rewriting a fact's text but keeping its old embedding (LightMem).
Facts derived from an LLM narrative instead of raw turns (EverMemOS), and extraction on a closed hosted service (Memori).
In-process write buffers that are lost on a crash (LightMem; our own window queue today).
